Spach |Narcissus recurvus|Haw. |Narcissus tripedalis|Lodd. ex Schult. & Schult.f. |Narcissus tripodalis|Salisb. ex Herb. |Stephanophorum purpuraceum|Dulac }} |synonyms_ref = [http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-282063 The Plant List] }} '''''Narcissus poeticus''''', the '''poet's daffodil''', '''poet's narcissus''', '''nargis''', '''pheasant's eye''', '''findern flower''' or '''pinkster lily''', was one of the first [[daffodil]]s to be cultivated, and is frequently identified as the narcissus of ancient times (although ''[[Narcissus tazetta]]'' and ''[[Narcissus jonquilla]]'' have also been considered as possibilities). It is also often associated with the [[Greek mythology|Greek legend]] of [[Narcissus (mythology)|Narcissus]]. It is the [[type species]] of the genus ''[[Narcissus (plant)|Narcissus]]''. ==Description== The flower is extremely fragrant, with a ring of [[tepal]]s in pure white and a short corona of light yellow with a distinct reddish edge.{{cite book|last=Woodhead|first=Eileen|author2=William W. Custead|title=Early Canadian Gardening|publisher=McGill-Queen's Press – MQUP|year=1998|page=171|isbn=978-0-7735-1731-8}} It grows to {{convert|20|to|40|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall.{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220008994|title=Narcissus poeticus|work=Flora of North America|access-date=2008-12-25}}[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358308#page/301/mode/1up Linnaeus, Carl von. 1753. Species Plantarum 1: 289, ''Narcissus poeticus'']Rafinesque, Constantine Samuel. 1838. Flora Telluriana 4: 20, as ''Autogenes angustifolius'' and ''Autogenes poeticus'' ==Taxonomy== ''Narcissus poeticus'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his book ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' on page 289 in 1753.{{cite web |title=Taxon: Narcissus poeticus L. |url=http://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?25042 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151223074228/https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?25042 |archive-date=23 December 2015 |publisher=ars-grin.gov ([[Germplasm Resources Information Network]]) |access-date=15 December 2015 }}{{cite web |title=Amaryllidaceae Narcissus poeticus L.|url=https://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=66165-1 |publisher=ipni.org (International Plant Names Index) |access-date=15 December 2015}} ==Distribution== ''Narcissus poeticus'' is native to central and southern Europe from [[Spain]], [[France]] through [[Switzerland]], [[Austria]], [[Slovenia]] to [[Croatia]], [[Albania]],The Edinburgh Philosophical Journal - Vol.18 - Pag.51 [[Greece]] and [[Ukraine]].Peter Hanelt (Editor) for Institute of Plant Genetics and Crop Plant Research {{google books|10IMFSavIMsC|Mansfeld's Encyclopedia of Agricultural and Horticultural Crops: (Except Ornamentals)|page=227}} It is naturalised in [[Great Britain]], [[Belgium]], [[Germany]], the [[Czech Republic]], [[Azerbaijan]], [[Turkey]], [[New Zealand]], [[British Columbia]], [[Washington (state)|Washington state]], [[Oregon]], [[Ontario]], [[Quebec]], [[Newfoundland]], and much of the [[eastern United States]],Pugsley, Herbert William. 1915. Journal of Botany, British and Foreign 53 (Suppl. 2): 36, as ''Narcissus hellenicus''Sell, Peter Derek. 1996. Flora of Great Britain and Ireland 5: 363, as ''Narcissus poeticus'' subsp. ''majalis''Dulac, Joseph. 1867. Flore du Département des Hautes-Pyrénées, 133, as ''Stephanophorum purpuraceum'' from [[Louisiana]] and [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] north to [[Maine]] and [[Wisconsin]].[https://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=282063 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families][https://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Narcissus%20poeticus.png Biota of North America Program] ==Legend and history== [[File:Gc24 narcissus pseudonarcissus and poeticus.jpg|thumb|right|Botanical drawing, {{circa|1659}} (''N. poeticus'' in center)]] [[File:Illustration Narcissus poeticus0.jpg|thumb|right|Botanical drawing from [[Otto Wilhelm Thomé]]'s ''Flora von Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz'' (1885)]] The earliest mention of poet's daffodil is likely in the ''Historia Plantarum'' (VI.6.9), the main botanical writing of [[Theophrastus]] (371 – {{circa|287 BCE}}), who wrote about a spring-blooming narcissus that the [[Loeb Classical Library]] editors identify as ''Narcissus poeticus''.{{cite book|last=Jashemski|first=Wilhelmina Mary Feemster|author2=Frederick Gustav Meyer|title=The Natural History of Pompeii: A Systematic Survey|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2002|page=131|isbn=978-0-521-80054-9}} According to Theophrastus, the narcissus (νάρκισσος), also called leirion (λείριον), has a leafless stem, with the flower at the top. The plant blooms very late, after the setting of Arcturus about the equinox.Theophrastus, ''Historia plantarum'' (''Enquiry into plants''), ed. A. Hort, vol. 2, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1916 (2:1961), p. 42-43. "ὄψιον δὲ σφόδρα· μετὰ γὰρ ᾿Αρκτοῦρον ἡ ἄνθησις καὶ περὶ ἰσημερίαν". The poet [[Virgil]], in his fifth ''[[Eclogues|Eclogue]]'', also wrote about a narcissus whose description corresponds with that of ''Narcissus poeticus''.{{cite book|last=Bourne|first=Stephen Eugene|author2=W. L. Foster|title=The Book of the Daffodil|publisher=J. Lane|year=1903|page=[https://archive.org/details/bookdaffodil00bourgoog/page/n18 3]|url=https://archive.org/details/bookdaffodil00bourgoog|quote=the book of the daffodil bourne.}} In one version of the myth about the Greek hero [[Narcissus (mythology)|Narcissus]], he was punished by the Goddess of vengeance, [[Nemesis (mythology)|Nemesis]], who turned him into a Narcissus flower that historians associate with ''Narcissus poeticus''.{{cite book|last=Lehner|first=Ernst|author2=Johanna Lehner|title=Folklore and Symbolism of Flowers, Plants, and Trees|publisher=Omnigraphics|year=1990|page=73|isbn=978-1-55888-886-9}}"In the classic myth, Nemesis, the deity of vengeance, complying with [[Hera]]'s order to punish Narcissus for his [[egotism]], turns him into the narcissus flower (''narcissus poeticus'')" Peavy, p. 438.{{cite journal|last=Peavy|first=Charles D.|date=Jul–Sep 1966|title=Faulkner's Use of Folklore in The Sound and the Fury|journal=The Journal of American Folklore|volume=79|issue=313|pages=437–447|jstor=537508|doi=10.2307/537508|publisher=American Folklore Society}} The fragrant ''Narcissus poeticus'' has also been recognised as the flower that [[Persephone]] and her companions were gathering when [[Hades]] abducted her into the [[Greek Underworld|Underworld]], according to [[Hellmut Baumann]] in ''The Greek Plant World in Myth, Art, and Literature''. This myth accounts for the custom, which has lasted into modern times, of decorating graves with these flowers.Taken from Baumann, Hellmut, ''The Greek Plant World in Myth, Art, and Literature'', London: The Herbert Press; 1993. Cited in {{cite journal|last=Dafni|first=Amots|author2=Efraim Lev |author2-link=Efraim Lev|author3=Sabine Beckmann |author4=Christian Eichberger |date=2006-09-10|title=Ritual plants of Muslim graveyards in northern Israel|journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine|volume=2|issue=38|doi=10.1186/1746-4269-2-38|page=38|pmid=16961931|pmc=1584233 |doi-access=free }} [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]], who gave the flower its name, quite possibly did so because he believed it was the one that inspired the tale of Narcissus, handed down by poets since ancient times.{{cite web|url=http://www.floridata.com/tracks/misc/daffodils.cfm|title=Daffodils – the Flower that Means Spring!|last=Allen|first=Ray|work=Floridata|access-date=2008-12-26}} ==Uses== In medicine, it was described by [[Dioscorides]] in his ''[[Materia Medica]]'' as "Being laid on with Loliacean meal, & honey it draws out splinters".{{cite web|url=http://www.rcpe.ac.uk/library/history/physic-garden/physic-garden.php|title=The Sibbald Physic Garden|last=Eastwood|first=Dr M A Eastwood|work=History of Medicine|publisher=Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh|access-date=2008-12-26}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}} James Sutherland also mentioned it in his ''Hortus Medicus Edinburgensis''.{{cite journal|last=Robertson|first=Forbes W.|date=Winter 2001|title=James Sutherland's "Hortus Medicus Edinburgensis" (1683)|journal=Garden History|volume=29|issue=2|page=144|jstor=1587367|publisher=The Garden History Society|doi=10.2307/1587367}} In [[Korea]], it is used to treat [[conjunctivitus]], [[urethritis]] and [[amenorrhoea]]. ===Use in perfume=== Poet's daffodil is cultivated in the [[Netherlands]] and [[southern France]] for its [[essential oil]], narcissus oil, one of the most popular fragrances used in [[perfume]]s. Narcissus oil is used as a principal ingredient in 11% of modern quality perfumes—including 'Fatale' and 'Samsara'—as a floral concrete or absolute. The oil's fragrance resembles a combination of [[jasmine]] and [[hyacinth (plant)|hyacinth]].{{cite book|last=Groom|first=Nigel|title=The New Perfume Handbook|publisher=Springer|year=1997|page=225|isbn=978-0-7514-0403-6 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UYrDPqLVD-kC&q=%22narcissus+poeticus%22+perfume&pg=PA225}} ==Cultivation== ''Narcissus poeticus'' has long been cultivated in Europe. According to one legend, it was brought back to England from the [[crusades]] by Sir Geoffrey de Fynderne.{{cite book|title=The Christian|publisher=Morgan and Scott|year=1871}} It was still abundant in 1860 when historian [[Bernard Burke]] visited the village of [[Findern]]—where it still grows in certain gardens and has become an emblem of the village.{{cite web|title=Welcome to Findern|url=http://www.johnport.derbyshire.sch.uk/FindernPC/index.html|work=Findern Parish Council|access-date=2008-12-26}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}} It was introduced to America by the late 18th century,{{cite book|last=Taylor|first=Raymond L.|title=Plants of Colonial Days|publisher=Courier Dover Publications|year=1996|page=68|isbn=978-0-486-29404-9}} when [[Bernard McMahon]] of [[Philadelphia]] offered it among his narcissus. It may be the "sweet white narcissus" that [[Peter Collinson (botanist)|Peter Collinson]] sent [[John Bartram]] in Philadelphia, only to be told that it was already common in [[Pennsylvania]], having spread from its introduction by early settlers.Ann Leighton, ''American Gardens in the Eighteenth Century: 'For Use or for Delight' ''(University of Massachusetts Press) 1986:459. The plant has naturalised throughout the eastern half of the United States and Canada, along with some western states and provinces.{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=NAPO|title=Narcissus poeticus L.|work=USDA Plants Profile|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture|access-date=9 January 2013}} ''Narcissus poeticus'' has long been hybridised with the wild British daffodil ''[[Narcissus pseudonarcissus]]'', producing many named hybrids. These older heritage hybrids tend to be more elegant and graceful than modern hybrid daffodils, and are becoming available in the [[UK]] once again.{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3347251/Narcissus-Old-gold.html|title=Narcissus: Old gold|last=Kingsbury|first=Noel|date=2008-03-20|work=telegraph.co.uk|access-date=2008-12-26}} One such cultivar is the popular 'Actaea', which has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/96914/Narcissus-Actaea-(9)/Details | title = ''Narcissus'' 'Actaea' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 18 February 2020}} ''N. poeticus'' var. ''recurvus'', the old pheasant's eye daffodil, has also won the AGM.{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/76534/Narcissus-poeticus-var-recurvus-(13)/Details | title = ''Narcissus poeticus'' var. ''recurvus'' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 24 February 2020}}{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 107 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | website = www.rhs.org | access-date = 18 February 2019}} ==Toxicity== While all narcissi are poisonous when eaten, poet's daffodil is more dangerous than others, acting as a strong [[emetic]] and irritant.{{cite book|last=Hanks|first=Gordon R.|title=Narcissus and Daffodil: The Genus Narcissus|publisher=CRC Press|year=2002|page=27|isbn=978-0-415-27344-2}} The scent can be powerful enough to cause headache and vomiting if a large quantity is kept in a closed room.{{cite book|last=Grieve|first=Maud|author2=C. F. Leyel|title=A Modern Herbal|publisher=Courier Dover Publications|year=1971|page=573|isbn=978-0-486-22799-3|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KgfHxvGFHAoC&q=Grieve+%22A+Modern+Herbal%22+poeticus&pg=PA573}} ==Photo gallery==
